en: Preface to the *Qionglou Yingao* (Drafts from the Jade Tower).
On the eve of the full moon in the second month of the Gengzi year, the Master of Er-lin returned south from his official duties and visited his elder brothers' sons.
When he inquired after the illness of Mr. Tao of Qionglou, they informed him that he had already passed away twenty days prior. Thereupon, [the Master] offered a bowl of clear water.

I composed a text to offer a sacrifice to a single blossom of the plum tree. Subsequently, while examining his remaining manuscripts, I found ten poems he had written in response to my own "Poems on Closing the Gate" from previous years.
Having read them, I sighed and said: "How extraordinary! This is the voice of the kalaviṅka bird.

In the Western Buddha-land, amidst the groves of the seven treasures, their harmonious songs are mournful and elegant, producing sounds that call to mind the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha. Its...
"Is it here? Is it indeed here? He then completely brought forth all the poems he had composed throughout his life; totaling several volumes, he edited them and retained some ninety-odd pieces.
He preserved their original titles and called the collection *The Drafts of Poems from the Jade Tower* (*Qiónglóu Yínǎo*).

When he first began writing poetry, he expressed his sentiments through wind and flowers and cultivated his emotions amidst mountains and waters; his diction was pure and remote, untainted by worldly dust. As he grew slightly older...
By reading the writings of the sages, worthies, Buddhas, and patriarchs, one gradually learns to prune away flowery rhetoric and urge oneself toward the inner essence.

Is there not one who is intent upon the ancient way of learning for the sake of self-cultivation? Upon reaching the composition of ten poems, one penetrates the source of the Dharma, purifies all doubts, and allows the latent power of many lifetimes to burst forth from the tip of the brush.
This is not something that those of shallow wisdom and meager faculties can possibly fathom or recognize.
Thus it is. Reading the poems of Qiong-lou, one person regards him as a man of talent, another as a high-minded gentleman, and yet another as a man of the Way.
Yet Qiong-lou himself is like a flower in the sky or a moon in the water—neither identical nor different, neither "I" nor "he.
To contemplate him in this manner, one may say that Qiong-lou dwells eternally even now. Preface by Peng Shaosheng.
An Annotated Excerpt from the *Qinglou Yingao* (Drafts from the Jade Tower),
compiled by Tao Shanqingyu of Changzhou; excerpted by a disciple of Hai Tian Jing She, Song (Jichou).

The cold wind whistles through ten thousand ravines; a crescent moon hangs over the eastern peak. Majestic are its sky-reaching trunks; dense and towering is its earth-piercing form. How could it not uphold the integrity of a nobleman?
Would it ever accept the title of a common official? While all other trees wither away, its dragon-like branches grow ever deeper in green.

Wax-plum blossoms appear at the close of the three winter months; clustered in pale yellow before the courtyard, they do not fall though the cold wind blows. When the warm sun shines upon them, their fragrance returns.
A thousand branches of jade-medicine emerge, yet within each lies a single point of crystalline heart. Dwelling serenely within the empty valley, one need not emulate the finery of the Han palace.

Camellia buds defy the snow, appearing like several points of rosy clouds; deep and light, they reflect against the window gauze. After the Master Mei finished his verse, the Master Su took up the pen;
it is the Sichuan tea that can endure the chill of spring.
The beauty of the plum blossoms surpasses that of all cities and states; who else can compare? Adorning herself before the morning mirror, she reveals a springtime unique to her own.
She smiles in contrast to the tens of thousands of wild peach trees, which lack the refined spirit found in her simple elegance.
I have heard that the fragrance of the *zhūizǐ* (shrub rose) wafts early from the Jade Palace; not only can its hue boast of surpassing the Fánchuān region.
Tonight, amidst the bright moon over Gūsū, who else shall compose verses on the *zhūizǐ* flower?
To season a soup with water-mallow, why must one think of the thousand-li journey? To gather the *mao* grass, what need is there to trace back to the *pan* palace?
With its silken fragrance lingering for three or four months on a single chopstick, this poem was originally not written for the autumn wind.
Litchis with skin as white as jade, rolled like honey-balls—what year did they fly on horseback to Chang’an? When Xing Zhi saw them, a single smile became a lifelong regret;
the catalog by Chen Junmu is too painful to bear looking upon.
Ginger is a garden vegetable that can eliminate evil; its meat-like flavor is excellent for sharing at the table. One must know that its pungent vigor comes from its natural disposition;
even the "cypress-thief" would find his gall chilled upon hearing this.
The cold weather heralds the coming snow; from a thousand peaks, the northern winds mingle. Frozen clouds first emerge from the ridges, and cold birds gradually return to their nests.

The fire is kindled and tea may be brewed; the poem is finished and its lines are ready to be chiseled. I call for my boy to bring the broom and wait, for the thatch is falling from the eaves outside the window.
Inscribed on a Painted Fan:
Mountains recede and forests stretch afar, the river’s surface is level and still. At twilight, clouds break across the sky as several peaks stand out in silhouette.
Within this scene dwells just such a traveler of mist and clouds; A lone boat glides lightly upon the setting sun.

A parrot from the Long Mountains, with its unconventional style and fresh adornment, Mistakenly entered a small jade hall at the edge of the world. One dream called back the foundations of the Tang dynasty;
For a thousand autumns, it has preserved the literary legacy of Han. On the slanting balcony, it learns to speak as the spring breeze is fine; At the curved railing, it calls for tea at dawn.

Incense of the seal-script style burns; where can this desolate, wandering melancholy find solace? Amidst the shadows of the swing and beside falling blossoms, I dwell in seclusion on a spring day (Gengyin).
In this small courtyard, there is much of a secluded charm:
leaning against the railing, the fragrant grasses grow level with the ground; in the spring breeze, several swallows return; and at sunset, a single cock crows.
Bamboo colors by the bamboo window to the north; Bamboo fragrance in the flower grove to the west. Who is as leisurely as I? The fisherman before the front creek.
An Impromptu on an Autumn Day, Taking a Walk: The grass in the pond is entirely yellow. A day of refreshing air, with cool breezes at noon. Still weary of cotton clothing after my illness.
Thin. Only upon waking from sleep do I realize that autumn days are long. A flowing stream and a small bridge; willows grow old. White clouds in a deep courtyard; osmanthus flowers are fragrant.
Across the neighbor’s wall, whose daughter is at her loom? She labors in her cold window, accompanied only by the setting sun.

At the end of autumn, the Su Terrace is cold with frost as geese fly south; Vastly spread, the yellow chrysanthemums play with their evening fragrance. In the evening rain, one idly listens to the flute atop the jade tower;

In the autumn wind, the golden scissors are too weary to cut the robes. The green leaves of the courtyard locust trees fall with a whistling sound; The butterfly’s wings unfold yellow as it flutters by.
A flight of birds; it is most refreshing for the year. Deep waters, slender mountains, and sparse white clouds.
Ascending Qionglong Mountain (Xinmao Year), the world beyond the secular realm is distinct:
the world within these mountains is pure. Pine roots coil around protruding rocks; bamboo shoots grow amidst the clouds.
Ascending Tianping Mountain, a thousand peaks stand steeply;
a single stream flows deep through the springs. Pausing to seek the ancient path, the small trail is strewn with red fallen blossoms.
Listening to the spring.
The old crane’s cry is especially bitter; the lone ape’s song is even more sorrowful. How can they compare to a single mountain stream, falling freely through the autumn of ten thousand peaks?
When sitting alone in my lofty chamber, I constantly admonish this mind: by maintaining only a single quality—patience—one may remain free from the encroachment of calamity.
Once at peace, do not be greedy; wealth and honor merely weary the body. Heaven and earth have their cycles of waxing and waning; how much more so for you, a man of fame and profit?
Reading books amidst deep fallen leaves in the empty mountains, as the returning light enters the pine trees—sweeping the stones, what do you intend to achieve? Read books simply to amuse yourself.
The flavors within this place are also extraordinary; day by day, one exchanges for new delights. Looking back, all is cool and serene: a crescent moon emerges from the mountain peak.
At the end of autumn, the sky is filled with a refreshing chill. Through the empty window, the moon first arrives. Between one or two thatched cottages lie two or three scrolls of ancient books.

The ink-well pool is filled with autumn dew; the bamboo path retains its evening fragrance. The birds on the sandy bank are carefree and untrammeled—surely even the *yuánluán* phoenixes cannot rival them.
Winter Day: Occurrences upon Entering Winter I have ceased my embroidery; sitting idly by the brazier, I chant verses. Pine seeds fall upon the cold inkstone; plum blossoms face the ancient zither.
Dust and grime vanish with worldly affairs; ice and snow clarify my heart. I ask those who have fled to Chan: where can one truly find it? *Yebu* (Renchen):
The splendor of the scenery passes in the blink of an eye; in the wilds, I lean on my staff, every step entering the profound. On the morning islet, plum blossoms mingle with the lingering snow.

Falling petals; the spring river carries clouds as it flows over broken ice. In several households among the woods and ravines, woodsmen ply their axes; at a wine shop, a single scroll of painted scenery is for sale.
Where else can this leisurely sentiment be lodged? Neither of this age nor of antiquity, I wander at ease as I please.

Living in seclusion, living in seclusion—the world and its heavens are renewed. In speech and silence, I follow my natural spontaneity. Flowers and birds become my companions; clouds and mountains are fit for a neighbor.
I sleep by day in a warm thatched cottage; I stroll idly on a grassy bridge in spring. Unconsciously, all worldly anxieties vanish; with such lofty aspirations, with whom can they be discussed?
Three Poems on the Scene in an Autumn Chamber The curtains stir with a gentle breeze;
A fresh coolness settles within the chamber. The autumnal scenery on this single courtyard is exquisite; The bright moon rests upon the wutong trees.
The summer heat has retreated and the inner chambers are pure; coolness arises as the autumnal round fan is used. With a mind clear and free from affairs, there is no need to speak of idle sorrows.
(In poetry concerning the inner quarters, it is rare to find such freedom from affliction.)
The day is long and the curtains hang to the ground; the incense has faded as the sun’s shadow turns back. Tugnuts fall upon the steps; one knows they were carried there by birds.
Unable to sleep, the night grows deep yet slumber does not come; I open the window and pace the small pavilion. The vast sky hangs with the bright moon; the autumn waters reflect the sparse stars.
Having attained the mind of constant joy, the firefly’s dream is naturally stilled. The western wind knows my intent; it rolls up the net and releases the drifting sails.

Ascending the tower for a late view, heaven and earth—how can they ever be exhausted? Human life is just like this: a long wind blows through the severed clouds as the sun sets into the waters of the Wu River.
The ancient sages do not remain today; who else now reflects upon self-restraint? Turning my head, the evening smoke stretches across the sky, and the bell from the distant temple begins to toll.
*Gengye jingshan yehua* (Night Talk on a Quiet Mountain with My Sister, Gui-si Year):

Dwelling in seclusion together amidst the spring chill, we lift our lamps to speak for you: In the vast space between heaven and earth, what distinction can there be between the clever and the clumsy?
The clumsy man is ever joyful; the clever man is bound by a hundred anxieties. The Great Way is fundamentally impartial; the white clouds are naturally at ease. In silence, both have forgotten words;
the realm of man is remote, pure, and absolute. A single dog barks through the deep watches of the night; the thatched gate is closed against wind and snow.
What is there when one steps outside?
What is there when one steps outside? A single stream of wildflower fragrance. Pointing toward a painting in the void, mountain after mountain is intoxicated by the evening sun.
Spring ends (Jiamu).

A night of wild winds has ended spring; forest flowers drift and settle across the rustic gate. Sitting by the flowing stream, my mind dwells nowhere; facing the green mountains at my door, even my dreams are at ease.
To study the Way, there is no need to involve oneself in worldly affairs; to cultivate the truth, why must one distance oneself from the human realm?
Rolling up the curtain, I point toward the path atop the peak; the solitary cloud, stretching out, can be grasped by hand.
Expressing My Feelings, Two Poems (Record One) I intend to go further to Mount Ni to inquire about benevolence;
I have heard the instruction never to follow what is contrary to ritual propriety. In Renchen, I first cultivated my nature by abstaining from wine;

In Dingyou, I polished my character with the intent to sever the consumption of meat. With a chest as white as snow, I dissolve worldly anxieties; Within the realm of the blue heavens, I recognize the True Nature.
This literary work. Within the curtains and embroidered hangings of my study, there is no difference from before;
yet my resolve to cultivate and refine myself grows doubly diligent. *Thirty Poems of Remorse* (with preface, Wuxu year).
During this long summer of leisurely dwelling, looking up and down at my station in the world, I feel my heart and ask myself: what kind of person do I wish to become? Now...
As women, we lack the means to extricate ourselves from body and mind; thus, we continue to drift through the cycle of birth and death.

As for our future lives, it would be impossible even to inquire about them. How perilous! How perilous! Fortunately, the true mind has not yet perished, and I have come to know a measure of shame and remorse.
When the mind encounters an object, its sentiments manifest in words. I have obtained several seven-character quatrains. The *Śāstra on the Explanation of the Sūtras* says:

"A person who lacks a sense of shame is no different from the various beasts. The *Taoist Scriptures* say: "For this reason, a sense of shame and remorse must not depart from the heart. Confucius said:
"In conducting oneself, there must be a sense of shame"—this is likewise the meaning of shame and remorse. Indeed, the sages and worthies of the Three Teachings [are in agreement].
To save others and to save oneself, both do not lie outside the foundation of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*). The common people abandon it;
the gentleman preserves it—it lies simply in this. While written chapters have their limits, shame and remorse are inexhaustible. Therefore, I have entitled this "The Verse on Shame and Remorse."
I feel shame that virtues from previous lives have not been cultivated; there are causes for these five obstacles to the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Yet, fortunately, I have obtained a human body—how could I still begrudge being a woman?
The three sacrificial animals and five tripods are not themselves extraordinary; how can one speak of filial thought without a sense of shame?
Having fortunately obtained a human body within heaven and earth, why must the repayment of this debt of gratitude be limited solely to men?

Alas for my parents, who underwent such great toil! How difficult it is to encounter the mind-to-mind transmission of the True Dharma. Though pointed out and roused by others, I have not yet attained realization;
I pity myself and feel ashamed as but a child.

The kindness of one's parents is fundamentally the same as that of heaven and earth; I am ashamed that the Way in my life has not yet been fulfilled. It requires only that one’s own mind be clear and penetrating;
then the four debts of gratitude will be complete, and one will realize the true void.
Whenever I rise at dawn and the sun has already grown high, I wipe my mirror and draw back the curtains, entrusting my handmaidens to provide me with bath and combing with diligent care.
Yet this body of mine sits here in shame, like a lifeless corpse.
At night, I most delight in my small brown couch; it is so pure, what need for various exotic incenses? I feel ashamed that the demon of sleep cannot be dispelled;
I must rely once more on the master within my dreams to exert his strength.
Crows cry as the sun sets; the beggar grieves. Sitting amidst the dew in the vast forest by the headwaters of a stream, I feel ashamed that I dwell in this Land of Peace and Bliss.
Cherishing life and knowing contentment, I shall strive diligently in my practice.
In the heat of summer, light gauze and thin silk; when winter comes, how warm are the emerald quilts! Such natural offerings are difficult to digest;
I am ashamed—I have never learned to weave even a single shuttle.
My neighbors also sigh over having no clothes; through their small windows, cold snow and sleet blow in.
I am ashamed that I have no ten-thousand-baggage of silk, yet I let all the warm air enter my thatched door.
In a poor household, even a升 (shēng) or a 合 (hé) of grain is difficult to procure; I feel shame and call out for relief, weeping by the roadside.
How can I obtain the *maṇi* wish-fulfilling jewel, so that it may rain down rice like pearls from the sky?
The hundred grains, various herbs, and fruits and vegetables—these were produced through the arduous labor of humanity. Now I feel ashamed that my belly is filled in vain;
I realize I have not attained even a taste of the flavor of Mount Ni.
The scriptures of the Three Teachings fill the heavens and the earth; who among them has recognized the true path? Even those with youthful faces and white heads must feel shame;
to transcend the world, one must indeed be a person of this world.
"Benevolence" is the human heart—its meaning is profound. At times, one boasts of literary skill and loses the true mind. Seeking the mind, one feels shame, for there is nowhere to find it;
one intends to seek it at the place where Yan Hui questioned [the Master].

Only through precepts and meditative concentration can wisdom arise; to casually boast of one's ability to feel shame and remorse is mere pretension. What purpose is served by shaving the hair and washing the marrow?
Even after awakening, one should not indulge in self-aggrandizement.
With firm power of mindfulness, I shall practice well; with abundant shame and remorse, my nature may be weak.
It would be better for my skull to shatter into pieces than that I should not ultimately achieve the patience of the non-arising of phenomena.
Grasping at the empty as if it were full, the mind is only then withdrawn. Reverence likewise arises from wisdom; shame and remorse lead one to constant self-exertion.
Having attained understanding through repentance and awakening, strive on!
Even Yao was weary of extensively bestowing bounty to relieve the masses; how could one who stands out and succeeds ever be at odds with the world?
It is not that shame and remorse should not be kept in mind at all times—the Sage is originally the teacher of those in training.

Purifying the faculty of the body is fundamentally not easy; first, one must abandon shamelessness, lack of remorse, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. The causal conditions of the three karmas are most subtle;
they directly teach that sprouts shall not grow wherever one touches.

To perceive that the very lifting of the mind is the point of error, and for the faculty of thought to become pure and return to the true source—one must know that all dharmas are ultimately non-dharmas.
Out of shame, I have spoken these words again without cause.

Purity of the six sense faculties is what is truly excellent; those who are as common as deer or driven by the winds of passion are merely my peers. With a heart full of shame and remorse, I have no attachments;
amidst white clouds and cultivated bamboos, I express my profound inner sentiments.
Together we stroll with our walking sticks among the fragrant flowers; in this refined gathering, zithers and chessboards reflect the night’s radiance.
With such matters weighing upon my heart, what else can I do? At the quiet window and clean desk, I add no incense.
I have broken the teapot to pass through the barrier of profit and fame; purple sashes and gold are but as trifles. With a sense of shame dwelling in my heart, I yearn for nothing;
beneath the clear wind and bright moon, I sit in the empty mountains.

A person of true cultivation must naturally find contentment in poverty; if one cannot find contentment in poverty, they will lose their true nature. With a sense of shame and remorse held in the heart, there is no suffering;
from the beginning, the study of the Way has been inherently arduous.
With few attachments to worldly conditions, transgressions are immediately dissolved; when insults and adversities come repeatedly, the mind remains at ease.
With a sense of shame held within the heart, there is no anger, even if glowing iron were to spin upon one’s head.
The ways of the world cause particular anxiety during times of inaction; to diminish and again diminish until one is beyond human knowledge.
Lately, I have come to realize the subtlety of this "diminishing," and I feel ashamed, sighing over the lost sheep at the parting of the paths.
The elegance of the inner chambers is adorned with rouge and powder; silks and brocades are dyed with the fragrance of musk and orchids. My heart feels ashamed and unable to follow the crowd;
with hair bound in a topknot and wearing a green robe, I emulate Meng Guang.
Alas, alas! Life is suffering, roasted and boiled; blood stains the knife and cutting board as it is made into daily fare. In shame, we cannot protect one another;
where will these vengeful spirits find relief from their abandonment?
The Rishi Kṣāntivādin practiced great giving; who would have known his asceticism of gouging out his own eyes?
Now that his compassionate vows are boundless, he feels shame for his past toil as his golden hands hang down.
Your golden hands hang down in emptiness, never wearying; your compassionate canopy covers humans and devas, yet those who encounter it are rare. This is the most shameful point of my current life:
that I have not yet joined the great assembly in taking full refuge.
O Gautamī, may your vows be vast and boundless; may you deliver all women of Jambudvīpa.
May you atone for the many obstructive karmas of past lives, yielding a spiritual illumination that precedes the awakening of others.
In the spring of the Wuxu year, while in retreat at the residence of the Master of Huilin, I compose ten verses following the original rhyme scheme (Jihai).
Within the light of formlessness, there is naturally the Real; the breeze of compassion sweeps through the four seasons of spring. Now, with a single stroke, all is extinguished.
Rest. Bow repeatedly as you dedicate [merit] toward the Lotus Land.
Originally there is neither reality nor emptiness; discussing the Way or expounding on Chan is merely a secondary matter.
With the single phrase "Amitābha," the empty self-nature is revealed: who is "I" and who is "another"?
The ice melts and the spring pond’s ripples settle; the myriad phenomena reflect in the void as the light of wisdom becomes perfect.
One must know that after practice is fulfilled and merit is accomplished, the warbling of birds and the fragrance of flowers are also spontaneous.
The pavilion overlooks clear waters; the house leans against the mountains. Amidst the shade of green vines, the pine gate is closed.
When you have leisure, take care to recognize the path home, lest you find yourself with nowhere to cling when the moment arrives.
The divine journey through the Pure Land is as bright as the sun; why use a staff to light a torch of bracken at night? To speak vaguely of the hundred and eight thousand paths is in vain;
the towers and pavilions in the void lie even further to the west.
How does this grove of trees differ from a forest of the seven treasures? Even upon its branches, one may hear the spiritual birds;
amidst the eastern breeze, they naturally preach the Dharma, producing hundreds of thousands of subtle and wondrous sounds.
Awake and alert day and night, look through to the very bottom. How many times life and death arise, all without cause. After the snow has fallen in the village ahead, the plum blossoms open;
The springtime radiance is revealed, impossible to conceal.
The scenery of the ninety days of spring easily turns desolate. A bright lamp illuminates the passage of the spring night. Brewing tea is not for its fragrance or flavor;
to suit one’s兴致 (xìng), what harm is there in drinking from a single ladle?
In this land, they have bound themselves by the covenant of the Lotus Society; from the waters of eightfold merit, lotus flowers bloom.
With single-mindedness and without distraction, they transcend the ranks of ordinary beings, resolutely proceeding toward the pure abode of the Land of Bliss.
Having penetrated the heavy barrier, truth is encountered everywhere; from now on, one shall not enter the old ford of delusion. The six characters of "saṃsāra" have no beginning or end;
flowing water and drifting clouds are all spring.
The third wife, née Táo, daughter of the Elder Wěi-Qí, was a granddaughter of Sūn Xīluó. She was fond of learning and skilled in poetry, while also cultivating the Pure Land practice.
She passed away at the age of twenty-five; these verses were written to mourn her. (By the Old Man of Xiāngshān) Her spiritual vocation was transcendent, perfected from her youth.
A single string of mani-jewels sufficed for her entire life. At the parting of ways, she stood firm and solitary, empty [of attachment].
All you who possess the [Buddha’s] marks, should go to the Western Pond to verify our old covenant.
You once transmitted the style of the Xie family in chanting about the floating willow catkins; I always cherish your mountain dwelling where the ten thousand sounds are empty.
I am filled with shame that my own verses have increased my power on the Path; my concern is not for the redness of falling blossoms (author: *Shanju tong cankui yin*).

An Inscription for the Sacrifice to My Niece’s Wife, Lady Tao (Master Er-lin) On the full moon day of the second month in the forty-fifth year of the Qianlong era, Master Er-lin offered a bowl of clear water and a single blossom of plum to the spirit of my niece’s wife, Lady Tao, saying: "Alas! This is water..."
It is not form; it is a flower that is not fragrance. Dependent conditions have no master; they abide eternally in the light of quiescence.
When a fleeting emotion arises, it blazes forth and ceases like wind passing through space, or like spring sweeping away the snow. Alas for your karmic wisdom, manifesting now in a female body!
Sandalwood is burned by day; the *muhua* beads are turned at night. With the *Dà bǎo'ēn jīng* (Great Sutra on Repaying Kindness), ink splashes across the pages.

My pure vows are firm and steadfast; may I long hasten toward the Ninth Grade. For fifty days upon my sickbed, for twenty years at the dressing table—I have now realized the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

Whence did I come, and whither shall I go? The bonds of beginningless craving must be severed from this moment forth. Within the pool of merit, flowers bloom in profusion. *Ruo...* (The text ends here).
The curtains are hushed; the spring watches grow deep. I bear witness for you: do not retreat from your original resolve. Alas! May you enjoy this offering.
A Brief Account of the Late Wife, Lady Tao:
Lady Tao’s name was Shan, her courtesy name was Qingyu. She was the eldest daughter of Gong Jixuan, a lifelong contributor to the Suzhou Prefectural School.
She was a girl who, from her youth, was intelligent and fond of reading. At the age of fourteen, she composed a poem on the "Hundred Flowers," which immediately won the admiration of the elders.
By nature, she possessed a powerful memory; she had extensively studied the classics and histories, and was able to recite from memory many types of reference works.

While attending to her parents, she served them with grace and joy, fulfilling their wishes and performing every ritual with meticulous care. At the age of sixteen, her grandfather arranged a marriage for her with Xi Luo. After eight years...
In her [marriageable] year, she first returned to me; she was two years older than I, being twenty-three at the time. She served my mother with such great success that she won her heart;
in her dealings with her sisters-in-law, there were no words of discord. She governed her maidservants and laborers with a balance of leniency and severity that met the proper measure.
Her own frugality and simplicity were even greater. My mother said to her relatives: "The temperament of my second daughter-in-law is much like my own. From that time on, I...
One may thus somewhat ease the mind’s burden. By nature, I have always been stern and impulsive, unable to tolerate others.

Since my wife returned home, she has constantly exhorted me to be broad-minded and compassionate in all matters; I, too, have deeply restrained myself, and my temperament has gradually become more even.

Last autumn, before the examinations, my wife urged me to apply myself to my studies and entrusted the management of household affairs to her, so that I was able to concentrate exclusively on my learning.

Regarding his studies for the civil service examinations and the subsequent trials and recommendations, he did not succeed. The lady comforted him with the principles of righteousness and destiny. At that time, the lady was pregnant;
in her daily conduct, eating, resting, and breathing, she always took the ancient methods of prenatal education as her model.

On the first day of the twelfth lunar month, Yunhui was born. She experienced the labor with great ease. The lady said to me, "I have yet to have a grandson; having obtained this [son] is a blessing."
One could have comforted her compassionate heart; yet who would have thought that after only half a month, she was suddenly overcome by the ravages of time?
Medicines proved ineffective, and as the New Year approached, it culminated in a final parting. Alas for the Lady! At the age of nine, she took delight in observing the fasts.

As she grew older, she heard the teachings on transcendence from her parents, read Buddhist scriptures, and attained a profound and lucid understanding of their meaning. She personally transcribed the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness).
His calligraphy for the *Vajra-amitābha-sūtra* and other scriptures was upright and well-proportioned.

Upon seeing my late paternal uncle’s various works, such as the *Treatise on the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* and the *Biographies of Lay Practitioners*, he subsequently dedicated himself to the Pure Land, establishing a daily routine of regular recitations. He would rise at dawn.
After finishing his cleansing and grooming, he would invariably recite the names of the Buddhas and various sutras and mantras.

Compassionate toward the excessive slaughter practiced by the customs of the Wu region, he printed one thousand copies of the *Cixin Baodian* (Precious Mirror of Compassionate Heart) compiled by Shen of Wujiang to distribute as gifts.

He once composed sixty stanzas of the "Verses on Shame and Remorse" (*Canjui Yin*), which his paternal uncle evaluated, saying: "Excellent roots; excellent faith and vows. Strive diligently in your cultivation."
He said, "It does not hinder one from manifesting the body of a great man to preach the Dharma. His uncle had granted him this permission in his heart.
One month before his death, he said to me, "My connection with you shall last no more than a year.
When I die, do not grieve for me. My regret is that I was unable to serve my aunt until the end of her life. If you have any regard for me, I hope you will comfort my aunt."
"Furthermore, it is my wish that you do not forget my parents. When my illness was at its worst, my maternal uncle and aunt came in person to examine me;
they did nothing but offer me consolation. At the moment of death, I chanted the Buddha’s name several times and the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha-mantra*, saying:
'The Great Monk comes from the West; I am going. Thereupon, I closed my eyes. Alas! Even now, the hanging remains..."
The new dressing table has suddenly been closed; turning back to look at the past, it is truly like a dream.

My lady was inherently endowed with the roots of wisdom from her youth, and at the moment of departure, she experienced no obstruction whatsoever. Yet, I reflect that I lost my father in childhood and have long grieved over my solitary reflection;
now, once again, the sorrow of losing my wife weighs upon my aged mother, further increasing her deep melancholy. How could I bear this?
Can one forget the lingering sorrow of the solitary dawn in light of the profound discourse of Master Tuo Da?
For this reason, I have briefly recorded the beginning and end of these events and appended them to the family chronicle, so that future generations may have something upon which to rely.
Lady Ru was born on the twenty-second day of the second month of the twenty-first year of the Qianlong era and passed away on the first month of the forty-fifth year of the Qianlong era.
The twenty-third day. At the age of twenty-five. One son: Yunhui. A period of mourning without the staff.
Recorded by Peng Xiluo.
